extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, philosophy, and social science (readers of Victorian-era reviews and theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical exposition and classification of emotions, feelings, cognitions, volition, and of the idea of society-as-organism; includes methodological criteria for studying emotions and social organization. The text both proposes classification schemes and diagnoses methodological defects in a prior work (Bain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural history of the emotions requires analysis aided by development
rubrics_metrics.description: "without analysis aided by development, there cannot be a true natural history of the emotions; and that a natural history of the emotions based on external characters can be but provisional."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper scientific account of emotions must not rest solely on descriptive/external characters; it should employ analytic methods and developmental (ontogenetic/phylogenetic) investigation to uncover origins and structure. Anti-pattern: treating descriptive, incidental analyses as sufficient "natural history."

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate comparative and analytical psychology into descriptive accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Bain "has written a Descriptive Psychology, which does not appeal to Comparative Psychology and Analytical Psychology for its leading ideas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative accounts should appeal to comparative (across species and races) and analytical (breakdown of processes) psychology as leading ideas rather than treating them as occasional additions. Omission of these methods yields incomplete organization and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cumulative, generational effects of habit in emotion formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits persistent in successive generations produce cumulative modifications; modifications produced by habit are "emotions in the making."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how repeated individual experiences, when occurring across generations, can organically modify the nervous system and produce nascent emotions (example: birds on newly-discovered lands acquiring fear of man over generations). Do not ascribe such changes solely to selective killing-off; consider accumulated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a clear distinction between volition and reflex/involuntary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition should not be defined so broadly as to include reflexes; example: withdrawal from scalding heat occurs "even when volition is antagonistic" and thus is not volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there is a continuum from reflex to voluntary action, definitions and analyses must preserve the broad contrast between voluntary acts and automatic reflexes. Anti-pattern: classifying sneezing, coughing, or involuntary withdrawal as examples of volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate sensation from emotion; use 'feeling' as the umbrella term
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'emotion' is commonly used for sentient states not a direct result of bodily action, whereas 'sensation' denotes direct corporeal impressions; if a wider word is needed, adopt 'Feeling' to include all sentient states not classed as Cognitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merging basic sensations with emotions. Scientific psychology should recognize sensation and emotion as distinct though analytically related; class mental states first into Cognitions and Feelings, then subdivide feelings into sensation vs emotion types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify cognitions into four subclasses (presentative, presentative-representative, representative, re-representative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitions are divisible into: Presentative cognitions (localizing sensations), Presentative-representative cognitions (perception involving ideas of associated impressions), Representative cognitions (relations among ideas, e.g., recollection), Re-representative cognitions (abstractions that stand for aggregates of experiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four-fold distinctions when analyzing states of knowledge/perception and their increasing abstraction: from concrete localization through perception and recollection up to abstract, re-representative thought. Examples: perception of an orange (presentative-representative), abstract reasoning (re-representative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify feelings into four parallel subclasses (presentative, presentative-representative, representative, re-representative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings parallel cognitions: Presentative feelings (sensations, e.g., eating), Presentative-representative feelings (many emotions like terror, where sensations arouse aggregated represented sensations), Representative feelings (ideas of feelings called up apart from external excitements, e.g., poet's evoked feelings), Re-representative feelings (complex sentiments not directly tied to objects, e.g., love of property, justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this parallel taxonomy to analyze emotional complexity and development: from simple sensations to complex abstract sentiments that are organized from represented groups of experiences. Use examples (terror, poetic feeling, love of property, justice) as illustrations of each class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize organic representations and inherited components of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions may include 'organic representations'—vague inherited feelings produced by nascent excitation of ancestral nervous patterns; example: an infant crying at a strange sight due to dim discomfort from inherited effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for emotions, include not only individually learned associations but also vague inherited or race-level representations that make emotions more indefinite in early development. This supports explanations of early fear responses before individual experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat social organization as growth arising from individual activity and economic forces (not manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies and their constitutions 'are not made, but grow.' Large social facts (e.g., regional division of labour) arise not by legislation or design but from individual pursuits and natural causes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze social structure as an emergent product of millions of individual actions and economic necessities (division of labour, industrial specialization). Avoid attributing primary causation to legislative design or single 'hero' actors except as proximate, not ultimate, causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess legislative or imposed social changes by their conformity to national character and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even changes produced by law or despotism, if real and permanent, 'grow' because they ultimately depend on national will or popular character; artificial impositions out of harmony with that character rapidly retrograde.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reforms or laws, test whether they align with the underlying sentiments/character of the populace; lack of deep social fit predicts failure or rapid reversal (examples: failed permanent changes after Cromwell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of incoherent or forced analogies between society and organism/mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies (Plato's mapping of faculties to social classes; Hobbes's Commonwealth as 'artificial man') often contain inconsistencies—e.g., mapping magistrates to joints while reward/punishment are nerves; abstractions are equated with persons—leading to indefensible classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies only when correspondences are coherent and functionally consistent. Avoid mismapping roles/functions (persons vs abstractions) and check that the analogy preserves logical relations rather than producing contradictory identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate psychological works for systematic organization and inclusion of developmental/comparative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that Bain's work, though meritorious in detail, is defective in leading ideas and lacks a systematic organization founded on the methods and criteria (analysis, development, comparative study) insisted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess theoretical works on whether they: (a) provide a systematic organization underlying particulars; (b) trace changes through individual development and across races/species; (c) relate isolated national traits to social circumstances; (d) treat habits and generational persistence as explanatorily central rather than incidental.
